At Sendagaya today there are, they say, only two or three nurseries left, shops kept by a family for some generations; but in those days this quarter was full of them.
Alongside the small hatamoto residences stood gardens of five hundred, seven hundred tsubo.
The garden of Heigorō, where Okita Sōji was convalescing, lay south of the mansion of Naitō Suruga-no-kami (today the Shinjuku Gyoen), with a waterwheel turning on the north side of the house.
Okita lodged in the shed.
(Am I going to die?)
That was a thing Okita had never once considered. Perhaps he was simply born of a stock made bright toward life.
He was no longer under a doctor's care.
Now and then Matsumoto Ryōjun, once head physician to the shogunate, sent a page or a pupil round with medicine, but even that came less and less often.
Chiefly he took only a dubious tuberculosis cure, the Hijikata family's own patent remedy called Kyorōsan, which Toshizō had left with him.
"It works,"

The medicine Toshizō had sworn by. Told so, flat, from Toshizō's own mouth, he somehow felt it must work, and though he would sometimes quietly throw away the Western-prescribed medicines of Ryōjun, this one he kept taking.
His elder sister Omitsu came every second or third day and nursed him.
Each time she came, Omitsu boiled up boar-meat and the like, bought from the game-butcher, out in the yard.
"Drink the broth too,"
and she watched over Sōji as he ate, never leaving his side. Let her look away, and he was like to throw it out.
"It reeks,"
and Okita got it down his throat as if swallowing it whole.
Meat he had no stomach for.
"Sōji, you simply must get well. The Okita house may have passed to Rintarō, but you are the only one of the blood,"
"Well, that's a surprise,"
Sōji, with his bottomless brightness, cocked his head a little to one side.
"What is?"
Omitsu, drawn in in spite of herself, could not help smiling.
"What is, you ask — it's that way you have of talking, sister. I don't think this illness of mine is anything so grand,"
"Indeed it is,"
"There — that's just it,"
Sōji burst out, and,
"you fret yourself sick over everything, sister, and it doesn't hang together at all. If you knew it was no great illness, there'd be no call to worry so,"
"Do you think not?"
"I'll get well. Surely,"
he said, as if of someone else. Whether he truly believed it, the bottom of this young man's heart alone was hard to read.
His appetite was gone now, one might fairly say, altogether, and even when he forced food down he could not digest it well.
"It has reached the bowels,"
Matsumoto Ryōjun told Rintarō and Omitsu.
Once it reached the bowels there was not one hope in ten thousand of recovery.
Aboard the Fujiyama-maru returning from Osaka to Edo, even Kondō, no physician,
(Sōji will not last long,)
had said to Toshizō. And yet aboard the Fujiyama-maru Sōji did nothing but crack jokes and laugh, though he found it a trial himself: "When I laugh the cough comes on after, and it's a nuisance."
After they were back in Edo, Kondō said to his wife, Otsune (after the surrender of Edo she withdrew to the Jōgan-ji at Hongō in Nakano village, outside the city),
──I never saw a man so wholly reconciled to living and dying.
It was not something Sōji had won by training; it must have been inborn. Sōji was, at this time, twenty-five.
The shed at the nurseryman Heigorō's at Ikehashi-jiri in Sendagaya, where Sōji lodged — though called a shed, strictly it was no shed, having been made over, with tatami and fitted doors put in.
The paper-screened window faced south, so the light was good.
When he felt a little better he would open the screen and gaze vacantly outside.
The view was no good. For twenty chō in front lay farmland, planted with daikon and the like.
The old woman who saw to his needs,
"You never do seem to tire of it, do you,"
she marveled; for so long a time would he look, in the same posture, at the same thing.
The old woman had not been told that this young man was Okita Sōji of the Shinsengumi, who had once made the loyalist rōnin of the capital tremble.
"Inoue Sōjirō,"
was the name they had given him. If it came out that he was Okita, the Imperial army would make trouble. It was truer to say that Sōji was in hiding than that he was convalescing.
The old woman knew his standing, at least: the younger brother-in-law of Okita Rintarō, a retainer of the Shōnai domain.
Omitsu too had told the old woman,
──In the long-house of the domain residence, an illness such as his, people take it ill.
It was a plausible story.

Omitsu's husband Rintarō, as has been touched on before, came of the Inoue Matsugorō house of the Hachiōji Thousand Guardsmen; he too was a pupil of Kondō's father Shūsai, took his license in the Tennen Rishin-ryū, and, entering as an adopted husband, carried on the Okita name.
This was because the heir of the Okita house, Sōji, was still a child.

Rintarō, after Sōji and the rest went up to Kyoto, became a trooper of the Shinchōgumi in Edo, and when the Shinchōgumi passed out of the shogunate's hands, belonged now to the Shōnai domain and lived in the long-house of its residence. He had a son, called Yoshijirō. That son's son is Kaname, and this line survives today in the city of Tachikawa. So much by the way.
In the last third of the second month of Keiō 4, the Shōnai lord, Sakai Tadazumi, quit Edo and returned to his province.
Behind him remained his house elders, disposing of the Edo residence and settling what business was left.
Okita Rintarō was of the party that stayed on, though sooner or later he would have to go to Shōnai in Dewa.
That day of the withdrawal from Edo would be the day of Omitsu's parting in life from Sōji, and Omitsu dreaded its coming.
At last it came.
It was in the fourth month. By chance, the third. On this day Kondō went himself to the Imperial camp at Nagareyama and gave up his two swords.
Of that Omitsu knew nothing. This morning she came rushing in, and,
"Sōji, we are going to Shōnai,"
she said.
Sōji's smile vanished all at once.
But at once it came back, the usual look of this young man, and,
"Is that so,"
he said, reaching a hand out from under the quilt. He was frightfully thin.
Omitsu looked at the hand.
For the moment she could not take in what it meant.
Sōji wanted his sister to hold that hand.
But Omitsu was in a fluster.
What was to become of the brother she was leaving behind in Edo?
Beside herself, Omitsu was tidying the room this way and that, only moving her hands and body.
Money was the one thing to be counted on, and she slid nearly all the allowance that had come to Rintarō under Sōji's quilt.
"It has all come so suddenly,"

and, weeping, Omitsu was packing Sōji's belongings into a great wicker trunk. Packing them could serve no purpose, yet she threw herself into that work alone. Even the Kiku-ichimonji blade Sōji had carried in Kyoto she stowed inside it.
Sōji watched his sister so, steadily, from his pillow.
(Even the sword packed away — what does she mean by it?)
Whether his sister's flurry amused him, his face did not smile; only his shoulders drew in.
Omitsu seemed to have no time to spare. It looked as though she must run straight back to the long-house of the residence and set off with her husband.
"Sōji, I'll leave you new underthings and loincloths here, in a pile. I can do your washing no longer, but keep the things next your skin always clean,"
"Yes,"
Sōji nodded like a boy.
"My husband says that going to Shōnai may mean war,"

"They say the samurai of Shōnai are a hard, bold breed. Is it true they boast that the domain's men at home won't use an umbrella even in the rain? I heard some such talk as a child; if it's true, they must be a stubborn lot,"
Omitsu would not take up the talk.

"They say that in the castle-town of Tsuruoka the morning sun comes up over Mount Haguro, and I hear it's very beautiful. But how far it is from Edo. When I think that even in so northern a country the morning sun rises in the east, it makes me want to laugh,"
"Really, this one —"
Omitsu seemed at last to unbend a little.
"The snow will have melted by now. On the mountains some may still lie. Either way, it'll be hard going on your feet, sister,"
"You, Sōji, need only worry about yourself,"
"When I'm well I'll come to Shōnai. If Satsuma and Chōshū troops come from the west, I'll hold the Oguni pass on the Rokujūrigoe by myself. And I'll bring Kondō and Toshizō along too,"
"Ho-ho…"
Talking with this brother, one somehow grew merry oneself.
"What can Kondō and Toshizō be doing about now? I hear Edo is ringed round with the Imperial army — Nagareyama is safe, surely?"
"Those two are sturdy folk, after all,"
said Omitsu, an odd thing to say.
Sōji laughed.

"That's just it. When he was in Edo, Kondō ate a sea-bream someone had sent, roasted even the bones, said, 'This is the sort of thing you crunch right up,' and chewed and ate the lot. That astonished me, I can tell you,"
"He has such a big mouth,"
Omitsu burst out too.

"Yes, yes. There can't be another mouth so big in all Japan. At a drinking-party in Kyoto, Toshizō would, of all things, sing you a hauta or two; but Kondō's turn was only to put his fist in his mouth and take it out again — and that was his party-piece,"
"Well!"
Omitsu brightened.
"And your party-piece, Sōji?"
"I've none —"
"That's your father's blood,"
"Far off, it is,"
said Sōji suddenly.
"What is?"
"My father's face. I was about five, so I remember it only faintly. What is one to make of such things?"
"Eh?"
"If one dies, does one meet again over there?"
"Silly,"
At this Omitsu understood at last what it meant that Sōji had his right hand out of the quilt.
"Sōji, you'll catch cold,"
and, saying so, she softly took the hand and tucked it back under the quilt.
"Get your strength back soon. Get well and take a wife,"
Sōji did not answer.
On his pillow, he only smiled. In Kyoto he had once known a faint love for the daughter of a town doctor next to the Geishū domain residence. It had come to nothing in the end.
(A strange thing.)
Sōji looked up at the roof-beam. He was thinking. Foolish stuff.
──If one dies.
So Sōji was thinking.
(Who will offer incense and flowers for me?)
It nagged at him, oddly. Foolish stuff, he thought, and yet his life, that had left behind no such person, came to seem a thing bitterly fleeting.
Okita Sōji died a little more than a month after this, on Keiō 4, the thirtieth day of the fifth month, in that shed, with no one by to tend him.
Death, it seems, came suddenly. He had crawled out onto the veranda.
There he lay pitched forward. He was clasping the Kiku-ichimonji blade.
By the tradition handed down in Okita Rintarō's house, he had been trying to cut a black cat that always came into the garden.
Unable to cut it, he died.

His grave is at the Jōdo-sect temple Senshō-ji in Azabu Sakurada-chō, the Okita family temple. His posthumous name is Kenkōin Jin'yo Myōdō Koji. The perpetual-memorial fee was five ryō — paid, later, by Omitsu and Rintarō after they came back to Edo.
Later the gravestone decayed and was rebuilt, in Shōwa 13, by Omitsu's grandson Mr. Okita Kaname, with a perpetual-memorial endowment of two hundred yen — no small sum for the time.

The present head of Omitsu's Okita house is Mr. Okita Katsuyoshi, of 3-16 Hagoromo-chō, Tachikawa City, Tokyo. There a short account, set down of Sōji's brief life, has been handed down. By whose hand it was written is unknown.

Okita Sōji Fusayoshi, in childhood entered the school of Kondō Shūsuke of the Tennen Rishin-ryū and learned the sword. He was of uncommon gifts. At twelve years of age he crossed blades with the fencing-master of the Abe domain of Shirakawa in Ōshū, and won the victory. Thereafter his name rang loud through the domain.

Sōji, in childhood named Sōjirō Harumasa, later changed it to Fusayoshi. When the Shinsengumi was formed in Bunkyū 3, at but twenty years of age he became first among the jokin, the vice-commander's aides of the Shinsengumi, and captain of the First Unit. Great were his exploits.
Yet Heaven's register granted him no length of years. Alas, on Keiō 4, Boshin, the thirtieth day of the fifth month, he died of his illness. (The original is in classical Chinese.)
On the twenty-fifth of the month before Sōji's death, Kondō was beheaded at Itabashi.

At that time Sōji was still on his sickbed. But this news never reached the ear of Sōji, nursing his illness alone at the eastern edge of Sendagaya, and to his last breath he believed Kondō alive and well.
When Toshizō learned of Kondō's death by rumor on the wind, he had already abandoned Utsunomiya Castle and, holding the Nikkō Tōshōgū, was threatening the Imperial army about Edo.
After that he fought from place to place, his troops swelling by degrees, and by the time he had come down to Aizu-Wakamatsu there were already over a thousand men under him.
These Toshizō named
"the Shinsentai,"
the New Corps.
By that time the custom of naming a body of troops not a "gumi" but a "tai" had become general.
His second in command was Saitō Hajime, once a jokin under the vice-commander and captain of the Third Unit, a miraculous survivor from the founding of the Shinsengumi.
For the fineness of his sword he had been called, since the Kyoto days, the Demon Saitō, and in that time he had likely cut down thirty men.

Yet he took not a single graze. Later he went to teach swordsmanship at the Tokyo Higher Normal School and other schools, and though third- and fourth-dan men swarmed at him together, he let not one so much as touch his wrist-guard.
In old age he became a schoolteacher at the primary school of Nakano in Yugi village, Minamitama district.
In the Kyoto days he had been merely strong, a man of no great flavor; but as he fought his way from place to place, somehow his character grew droll by degrees, and one day,
"Captain, I've taken a pen-name. From today, would you call me by it?"
he said. Asked what it was,
"Dakusai,"
— he was laughing. A young man, yet a name like a retired old man's.
Toshizō burst out laughing too and asked the reason.
"Whatever you say, I say yes to it. So — Dakusai, Master Yes,"
he said.
This name he used until he died.

Besides this Saitō, for another vice-commander Toshizō chose Matsumoto Sutesuke, a former corpsman and a distant relative of his, from Minamitama district in Bushū. A holder of the intermediate license, who had studied the Tennen Rishin-ryū under Satō Hikogorō — no man of brilliance, but one who, under a rain of bullets, would charge in first without a change of color. Diving into the thick of the Imperial troops, he would,
"Matsumoto Sutesuke of the Shinsengumi,"
without fail announce himself.
By such things this man's name came to be known even among the Imperial army.
